summary: Analyzes threats against the Geopriv protocol architecture, including protocol threats, threats from entities storing data, and the abuse of information Geopriv yields. It lists security properties that answer those threats as a reference for requirements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo analyzes how location information can be intercepted, falsified, stored insecurely, or misused. It lists security and privacy properties that Geopriv designs should consider.

questions: what are the threats to location privacy
what threats affect geopriv location information
subtitle: Threats to location information in transit, in storage, and through misuse by authorized recipients.

tldr.problem: Location services can expose a person's current position, routines, and associations, and the Geopriv architecture must work across varied devices and relationships.
tldr.mechanism: The memo categorizes protocol, host-storage, and usage threats, then derives security and privacy properties intended to address them.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3694 is an Informational threat analysis, not a protocol specification. The unit metadata lists RFC 6280 as updating it.

today: RFC 3694 is an Informational threat analysis published in February 2004 and was updated by RFC 6280. It does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why Location Information Needs Protection
sections.content:
Location-based services can help people determine their own location and the location of others. Records of location exchanges can reveal habits, whereabouts, and associations. The Geopriv architecture is intended to support many kinds of location information, devices, relationships, and legal settings, which complicates protecting that information.

This memo analyzes threats to location information in transit and in storage. It notes that risks vary: a server selling information to marketers is different from an outsider intercepting someone's current location to carry out a physical attack. Some threats may be outside the Geopriv charter, but the memo includes them to identify useful security properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Location records can reveal where a person goes and who they interact with. The memo catalogs ways this information could be exposed or misused.

sections.title: The Geopriv Roles and Threat Actors
sections.content:
The architecture is expected to operate on the open Internet, where attackers may inspect packets, spoof addresses, and launch denial-of-service attacks. A Location Generator supplies location information to a Location Server. A Location Recipient requests or receives it, and a Rule Maker sets rules for its use. Connections between these roles create several places where information needs protection.

An attacker may seek a target's location, obtain more precise information than the Rule Maker allows, block or alter location data, identify a target's associates, or disrupt the system. The memo also considers authorized participants who may use or distribute location information outside agreed limits.
sections.plainLanguage: Location information moves between generators, servers, and recipients under rules set by a Rule Maker. Any of those parties or the network connections between them can be a source of risk.

sections.title: Protocol Attacks and Their Protections
sections.content:
An attacker may eavesdrop on a connection, impersonate a Location Server or Recipient, or pose as a Rule Maker to gain access to more precise information. The memo derives requirements for confidentiality on connections, authentication and authorization of recipients and servers, and authentication of Rule Makers.

Attackers may also spoof a Location Generator or replay an earlier location object to make a target appear somewhere else. The server must authenticate generators, recipients must authenticate servers, and the protocol needs replay protection. Traffic analysis can reveal who communicates with whom even when an attacker cannot read location content; the memo notes that this is difficult to address through protocol security alone.

A Location Server may become a denial-of-service target because it manages information for many devices. It may also amplify rapid updates by forwarding them to many recipients. Authentication operations can consume resources, so the memo calls for stateless authentication challenges and rules that limit the rate of location updates sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can read, alter, replay, or redirect location messages, and a central server can be overloaded. The memo calls for confidentiality, authentication, replay protection, and limits on update rates.

sections.title: Risks from Stored Location Data and Rules
sections.content:
Servers may accidentally send information to the wrong recipient, intentionally misuse it, suffer an intrusion, or be compelled to disclose records. Stored location information can reveal a history of where a target has been and with whom. Devices and viewers that retain logs create similar risks; information can also be seen on a screen, overheard through spoken directions, or exposed if a device is lost or stolen.

Rules can themselves disclose information. For example, a rule that degrades information by approximately 25 miles may help an observer infer the true location. Logs combined with knowledge of rules can also reveal more precise patterns or relationships.
sections.plainLanguage: Location information remains sensitive after it reaches a server, device, or viewer. Stored records and even the rules used to filter information can reveal a person's movements or relationships.

sections.title: Fair Information Practices
sections.content:
The memo says weak or missing default privacy rules can leave location information exposed. Users may not create rules themselves. Without defaults, a device could signal its location to nearby parties, respond to unknown requesters, allow redistribution, or retain information without limits.

It lists seven fair information practices: openness about collection and use; individual access and correction; collection limitation; accurate, complete, and timely data; use only for stated purposes; reasonable security safeguards; and accountability for compliance. The memo says default rules are necessary, although defining them is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Privacy rules should limit what is collected, how it is used, who can see it, and how long it is kept. Defaults matter because many users may not create their own rules.

sections.title: Security Properties for Geopriv
sections.content:
The memo recommends that Rule Makers define rules and that Geopriv provide default rules that at least limit disclosure and retention. A recipient should learn only the rules it must follow, and selected rules, such as when to delete data, should travel with the Location Object.

Short-lived identifiers and unlinked pseudonyms can support authentication without exposing participants' real identities. Rules may limit request frequency; the memo gives one request every 2 hours as an example for city-level location data. Connections need mutual endpoint authentication, location objects need integrity and confidentiality, and recipients or servers may need replay protection.

The RFC's Security Considerations section says it characterizes potential threats. Its IANA Considerations section introduces no additional IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Geopriv should let the Rule Maker limit disclosure and retention, use temporary identifiers where possible, and protect messages with authentication, integrity, confidentiality, and replay checks.

items.title: Openness
items.text: Explain that information is collected and how it is used.

items.title: Individual participation
items.text: Let people view and correct information about them.

items.title: Collection limitation
items.text: Collect only what is needed, fairly and lawfully.

items.title: Data quality
items.text: Keep information relevant, accurate, complete, and timely.

items.title: Finality
items.text: Use information only for stated purposes.

items.title: Security
items.text: Protect against loss, unauthorized access, and misuse.

items.title: Accountability
items.text: Make record keepers responsible for compliance.

references.text: Cuellar, J., Morris, J., Mulligan, D., Peterson, J. and J. Polk, "Geopriv Requirements", RFC 3693, January 2004.
